title: Participles

objectives.can: Parse present, perfect and future participles and say whom they describe.

explanation.summary: A participle is a verb that behaves like an adjective. It has tense and voice like a verb and it keeps its verb's object, but it takes case, number and gender from the word it describes. The Vulgate uses participles constantly, above all the present participle, because they translate the participles of the Greek of the New Testament.

sections.heading: Half verb, half adjective
body: Take *Jesum venientem* ('Jesus coming'). *venientem* comes from the verb *venio*, 'come', so it says that someone is coming. It also describes a noun and agrees with it, like an adjective: *Jesum* and *venientem* are both accusative singular masculine.

That agreement is the whole of the grammar of the participle. It looks at the word it describes, copies its case, number and gender, and tells the reader something about that word at the moment of the main verb. To parse a participle, give its tense and voice (what it says) and its case, number and gender (whom it describes).

sections.heading: Three participles
body: Latin has three participles in ordinary use. The present active participle, with -ns, -ntis, means an action going on at the same time as the main verb: 'coming', 'saying'. The perfect passive participle, in -tus, -ta, -tum, means something done before, with the subject on the receiving end: 'having been baptized'. The future active participle, in -urus, -ura, -urum, means something about to happen: 'about to hand over', 'about to come'.

There is no present passive participle, no future passive participle (the gerundive, which is a different thing, comes later) and no perfect active participle. A Latin writer who wants 'having done' must use another construction, or a deponent verb, which has a perfect participle that is passive in form and active in sense.

sections.heading: Declension
body: The present participle is declined like a third-declension adjective with one ending for all three genders in the nominative: *dicens*, *respondens*, with the stem in -nt- (accusative *-ntem*, genitive *-ntis*, nominative plural *-ntes*). Because the nominative is the same in the three genders, the library often shows the gender of a present participle as undecided.
The perfect and future participles are declined like *bonus*, *bona*, *bonum*, with endings -us, -a, -um, so the nominative alone does not give the gender in the plural or in the neuter.

sections.heading: A participle keeps its object
body: A participle is still a verb and can take an object, an adverb or a prepositional phrase. In *eum traditurus*, 'about to betray him', *eum* is the object of *traditurus* and is in the accusative. The participle agrees with Judas, the person it describes; the object does not.

sections.heading: Time is relative
body: A participle's tense is not a tense in the English sense. The present participle is 'present' in relation to its main verb, not to the speaker: if the main verb is past, the participle describes a past scene. In *vident Jesum ambulantem* the walking is at the same time as the seeing. The perfect participle is earlier than its main verb and the future is later.

misunderstandings: A participle is not a finite verb. *dicens* does not say who is speaking; it describes the subject of another verb, and the sentence has its own main verb.
The participle agrees with the noun it describes, not with the nearest noun. In *vidit Joannes Jesum venientem*, it is Jesus who is coming, not John, and the ending shows it.

Do not translate every participle by 'while ...ing'. A participle may express time, cause, manner or description, and the context decides. 'Having been baptized' is already a perfect passive; do not add 'was'.
Present participles in -ns are not always verbs: some, such as *sapiens* or *prudens*, are used as ordinary adjectives or nouns. The context shows whether the verb idea is still alive.

deeper.heading: Participles in the Vulgate
body: The Greek of the New Testament has a very large number of participles, and the Vulgate follows them closely. *respondens dixit* and *dicens* are formulas for 'answered and said' and 'saying', and they are constantly met in the Gospels. Classical writers would often have used a finite verb or a subordinate clause instead. Learning to see the participle as a clause (time, cause or description) is the first step to reading such Latin.

examples.analysis: *venientem* is a present active participle of *venio*, accusative singular. It agrees with *Jesum*, the object of *vidit*, and not with John, the subject: John saw Jesus as he was coming. The time of the coming is the time of the seeing.

examples.analysis: Two present active participles of *ploro*, both accusative. *plorantem* is singular and describes the woman (*eam*); *plorantes* is plural and describes the Jews who had come with her. The two forms show how the ending follows the noun's number.

examples.analysis: *traditurus* is a future active participle of *trado*: the stem of the supine *tradit-* with -urus. It is nominative singular masculine and describes the subject of *erat*, Judas, who was 'about to hand over'. *eum* is its object, in the accusative.
